specialist_findings.claim: Doctrine hierarchy is well-ordered: OWASP ASVS/Top 10, NCSC, and NIST supply-chain guidance are all named as primary sources at tier 1, before vendor docs and repo ADRs. This ordering is correct and aligns with how these bodies update at different cadences.

The doctrine hierarchy (lines 77-86) names OWASP ASVS and OWASP Top 10 but does not name OWASP SAMM or the Software Component Verification Standard (SCVS/CycloneDX). Given that dependency and supply-chain posture is explicitly in-scope (line 55), the absence of a named supply-chain verification standard means the delivered skill may anchor supply-chain assessment to informal hygiene rather than a testable standard. The plan should name at least one supply-chain-specific standard to guide the skill author.

The plan scopes in 'security observability posture (what should or should not be emitted, stored, or correlated)' (line 59) but draws no boundary with the named privacy-expert (line 68-70). Observability decisions about what to emit often turn on privacy-law requirements (GDPR Article 5 data-minimisation) as much as security posture. Without a stated join-point or escalation path, the delivered cyber-security-expert skill may make observability recommendations that conflict with the privacy-expert's doctrine or omit privacy-relevant constraints entirely.

The deployment context correctly identifies 'read-only by default' as a core safety posture and calls out the education context as raising trust-and-safe-defaults concerns beyond narrow exploitability (lines 94-96). This is appropriate framing for an LLM-agent-facing skill and does not introduce new security risk in the plan itself.

Secret lifecycle and credential-hygiene strategy is explicitly in-scope (line 56), but the deliverables list (lines 100-107) includes no validation step that tests whether the delivered skill actually surfaces secret-lifecycle gaps against a real scenario. Deliverable 6 is labelled 'Validation' with no content. A skill that claims to assess secret lifecycle without a proof-of-coverage check is a false assurance: it could omit short-lived token rotation, DI-seam credential injection, or .env leakage vectors and still pass a purely structural review. The plan should mandate at least one concrete scenario-based validation case for the secret-lifecycle and supply-chain remits before promotion.

Vercel deployment constraints are listed in scope (line 27-32) and repeated under Deployment Context (lines 49-55), but the deliverables (line 59-66) do not include a Vercel-specific integration test or smoke artefact. For a serverless Express deployment, cold-start behaviour and streaming are runtime concerns that cannot be fully validated by a static skill document alone.

specialist_findings.claim: Layer 3 proposes 'pnpm linear:emit-landing' as a skill-shaped command (PDR-009) but there is no PDR-009 alignment check on whether the skill boundary belongs in .agent/skills/ or the workspace package graph. The plan states 'canonical lives in .agent/skills/; adapters per platform' — this is a skills-not-packages placement that needs deliberate ratification under PDR-009 before execution, because workspace scripts that write to external services have different CI/DI concerns than purely repo-local skills.

The firing surface in Layer 3 is described as an agent-walked markdown ritual (session-handoff.md step 7c) rather than a deterministic code path. Layer 4 also explicitly states 'active means markdown-ritual, not code execution' for the health probe (citing PDR-029 Amendment Log 2026-04-21). PDR-029's two-complementary-layers principle is cited to mandate both a workflow gate and a health probe — but both layers end up as markdown ritual. This risks satisfying the letter of the two-layer requirement while leaving both layers in the 'ritual' category that Directive 3 (line 38-44) explicitly rejects. The architectural tension here is real and unresolved.

The local config boundary (.agent/local/linear.local.json, gitignored) is the correct PII pattern. However, the plan proposes a .env.example mirror entry for LINEAR_API_KEY (line 352) alongside a statement that 'MCP path avoids client-side keys' (risks table, line 432). If the MCP path is primary, the .env.example entry is a fallback that may never be needed and whose presence implies the SDK fallback path is a supported configuration. The architecture would be cleaner if the fallback condition for introducing a key were stated explicitly, rather than leaving both paths implied.

The architectural mapping table (lines 186-187) correctly distinguishes thread lifetime (indefinite) from issue lifetime (finite) and uses that to justify labels-not-issues. However, Option A in Phase 0.1.b (lines 261-266) proposes a 'rolling open issue per thread for the current landing target (mutated at each session)'. A rolling mutated issue has indefinite lifetime — the same lifetime property the plan uses to reject thread-as-issue. The tension between the mapping rationale and Option A is not surfaced; the plan recommends Option A without acknowledging this.

The one-way sync constraint (repo authoritative, Linear derived, no Linear-to-repo write) is architecturally sound and consistently stated throughout. The PII boundary (.agent/local/ gitignored) is a clean separation. The thread-to-label mapping satisfies the no-collapse directive (line 219) via Linear's own data model enforcement — this is a good use of the external system's constraints rather than an application-level invariant.

specialist_findings.claim: The plan assumes the tracked substrate study (source research file) exists and remains source-neutral, marked as a blocking prerequisite, but there is no first-hand verification that the file exists or that source-neutralisation was actually completed. If the study was never neutralised or was removed, the entire candidate pipeline has no evidence base.

The plan assumes C1 (feedback-loop-first diagnosis) and C2 (prototype expiry) are the highest-value candidates worth the first executable slice, but this prioritisation rests on the fit hypothesis alone with no documented evidence of repeated Oak failure modes for either. The 'Fit question' for both C1 and C2 is still open (lines 204, 219), meaning the strategic routing verdict 'promote to first Practice-fit review' is circular: it promotes candidates to a review that will decide if promotion is warranted.

The plan assumes 'ignored local source snapshot' is available for exact wording lookup (lines 318-319) but explicitly classifies this as 'Beneficial' rather than blocking. However, if the snapshot is unavailable, the fit review for candidates that require exact wording comparison (C1, C2) relies on a summarised neutral study rather than the primary source — a degraded evidence situation the plan does not fully acknowledge as a quality risk.

The sequencing assumption at line 30-41 names three prior plans that must complete or be resumed before this plan can be exercised (fitness-token-measurements plan WS1-WS6, cost-of-collaboration plan P8-A1 through P8-A4, completion-claim-proof-pipeline plan). The plan does not verify that these plans are themselves in a promotable state. If any of those plans stall, the sequencing assumption quietly defers this plan indefinitely without a stated timeout or re-evaluation trigger.

The plan assumes 'candidate count is not a success measure' (line 191) and correctly constrains the first slice to two candidates, but the strategic acceptance criteria (AC1, line 322) requires a fit verdict, natural home, and proof signal for each candidate before implementation. For C3-C8 (deferred or observe), no timing or evidence trigger is named for when they re-enter review — the assumption is that they will naturally surface again, which is not guaranteed.

The Foundation Alignment section (lines 386-394) assumes schema-first-execution constraints apply to any future validator for this plan. This is a reasonable carryover from the broader Practice but is stated as a given rather than verified against the specific validator shapes that C7 (inventory validation) would require. If the inventory validator's data model differs structurally from MCP runtime schemas, the constraint may need restatement.

specialist_findings.claim: The doctrine-scanner CLI output shape ({ file, line, pattern, citation, severity }) is deferred to promotion time, but the adaptive-immunity agent and practice-trio activation both depend on that structured output as their empirical base. Settling the schema at promotion of item 1 rather than at authoring time is defensible for a strategic plan, yet the dependency chain means any schema drift between promotion windows will require rework in items 2 and 3. An ADR capturing the output contract at promotion time for item 1 should be a hard gate, not a soft one.

The triggered rule loading pilot declares a `triggers:` YAML frontmatter block as the mechanism, but the loader hook that reads frontmatter and injects matching rules per turn has no specified integration point with the existing harness. The rule states the format is to be settled at promotion, yet the pilot is expected to run in parallel with items 1-3 (line 139-141). If the frontmatter loader lands before a stable harness integration contract exists, it risks producing a parallel loading path that conflicts with or duplicates the always-on rule loader, creating an architectural fork that is harder to collapse later.

The adaptive-immunity surveillance agent is classified as `process_executor` (line 296), consistent with ADR-135, but its output surfaces (fingerprint additions, calibration reports, vaccination samples) have no named consumer or home other than 'the practice'. Without a declared write-target — whether the fingerprint registry, the napkin, or a new artefact — the agent's outputs risk becoming ephemeral or written ad-hoc to wherever the agent finds convenient, which undermines the structural enforcement intent of the whole plan.

The non-goal at line 91-93 defers cross-platform parity beyond the adapter contract in ADR-125, but the doctrine-scanner CLI sketch at lines 268-276 describes a git pre-commit hook invoked via `pnpm agent-tools:doctrine-scan`. A pnpm-bound pre-commit hook is platform-coupled (Cursor, Claude Code, and other harnesses differ in hook execution). The sketch does not name the adapter seam that would satisfy the vendor-agnostic claim. This gap should be resolved before the CLI promotion gate is authored.

The Scope Expansion Register (items 1-4, lines 326-404) is well-maintained: three of four items have been promoted and landed, with exact commit SHAs and successor plan references. The register pattern here is sound and provides clean traceability. No architectural concern; noted as a positive signal for estate hygiene.

specialist_findings.claim: Assumption 1 asserts `.agent/state/collaboration/` is stable and is the coordination source of truth, citing P0-P2 cost-of-collaboration work having landed. The git status shows `.agent/memory/active/napkin.md` and `.agent/memory/operational/pending-graduations.md` as modified but no evidence the coordination surface files themselves have been verified as stable post-landing. The claim is directionally plausible but the cited evidence is indirect — P0-P2 landing does not itself prove the surface schema is frozen.

Assumption 3 states agent IDs encode a platform prefix (`codex:main`, `claude:peer`, `cursor:xyz`) and that this convention is stable enough to base dispatcher routing on. No ADR, schema, or enforcement mechanism is cited to guarantee this convention holds across sessions or across agents authored by different practitioners. The open question at line 25 acknowledges the gap but assumption 3 at line 332 then treats convention-stability as assumed, creating a contradiction: an acknowledged open question is simultaneously listed as a resolved assumption.

Assumption 7 states structured output is expressed only in the brief text, with the invoker responsible for parsing and validating. Open question 4 (line 38) explicitly asks whether structured output should be a `DelegationRequest` field or a brief-authoring concern, and names it unresolved. Assumption 7 resolves that open question inside the assumptions section without an owner decision marker, bypassing the promotion gate that requires owner decisions on all six open questions (line 308). This assumption is load-bearing for ClaudeInvoker design (Move 3, line 229) and contract stability (Assumption 4).

Assumption 6 assigns timeout enforcement solely to the dispatcher, not invokers. The risks table at line 324 notes 'means the dispatcher must be resilient to blocking calls' but lists no mitigation for that resilience requirement. If an invoker blocks indefinitely (e.g. a Codex process that does not terminate), the dispatcher's deadline enforcement requires either thread/process interruption or async cancellation — neither mechanism is addressed in the contract or dispatcher design. The assumption silently depends on a platform capability (cancellable async invocation) that is not verified for all platforms.

Assumption 4 treats the contracts as immutable once finalised, citing distributed-systems precedent and Anthropic SDK evolution as evidence. Anthropic SDK message format evolution is an example of a format that did change, which is the opposite of evidence for immutability; it is evidence that versioning is needed. The cited evidence argues for explicit versioning discipline, not for the assumption of stability.

The plan cites `cost-of-collaboration.plan.md (P0-P2 complete)` as a beneficial dependency but the plan file itself is not read here. The assumption that P0-P2 is actually complete and the coordination surface is production-ready (not merely landed) is unverified within this plan's scope. If P0-P2 work is in a broken or partial state, Assumption 1 collapses.

specialist_findings.claim: Two Must-Read Tier package README paths are wrong. The plan states `packages/core/env-resolution/README.md` and `packages/libs/eslint-plugin-standards/README.md`, but the actual filesystem paths are `packages/libs/env-resolution/README.md` and `packages/core/oak-eslint/README.md` respectively. The package names (@oaknational/env-resolution and @oaknational/eslint-plugin-standards) are correct, but an agent following the literal paths will 404. The in-scope table also lists @oaknational/eslint-plugin-standards under @oaknational/eslint-plugin-standards which is consistent with the package.json name, but the directory path given in the must-read tier is wrong.

Overlap boundary for test patterns (stubs vs fakes) is claimed as in-scope for ooce-expert (line 75: 'Test helper patterns (runtime stubs vs test fakes)') while the overlap table simultaneously assigns 'Package-specific test patterns (stubs vs fakes)' to ooce-expert and 'Test structure and TDD compliance' to test-expert. This is a deliberate split, but neither the plan nor the referenced testing-strategy directive (.agent/directives/testing-strategy.md, which exists) defines the handoff rule precisely. The boundary risks two specialists both claiming or both disclaiming a stub/fake question. The plan should cite the arbitration rule or add one.

ADR-129 (Domain Specialist Capability Pattern) is cited as the governing pattern at line 5, and the file exists on disk. However, the plan never cites or inherits any structural constraint from ADR-129 explicitly within its body — the pattern reference appears only in the header. If ADR-129 mandates a canonical deliverable shape (e.g. required SKILL.md sections, mandatory invoke-rule format), the plan cannot be verified for conformance without reading ADR-129 itself. No architecture finding is fabricated here; the gap is that the plan does not surface whether its deliverable list (lines 110-115) satisfies the pattern's requirements.

Deployment context (lines 100-106) names Turborepo as the build orchestrator and states 'Turbo handles this, but manual runs must respect the order' (line 65). This is accurate but the plan gives no guidance on what the specialist should advise when Turbo cache is stale or a developer forces a manual build outside Turbo. The codegen pipeline section (lines 49-67) only covers the happy-path ordering; cache-invalidation and out-of-order manual recovery are recurring agent mistakes not addressed as specialist scope.

All three deliverable artefact paths (ooce-expert reviewer template, SKILL.md, invoke rule) do not yet exist on disk — confirmed by filesystem check. The plan status is correctly marked NOT STARTED. No architecture defect; noting for completeness that the gap between the peer specialist estate (19 templates already landed) and this plan's zero delivered artefacts is consistent with future/ placement.
